strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and critical bottleneck of language-model-based 3D vision systems—inference speed—and achieves a substantial speedup of around 5x without sacrificing accuracy.

The adaptation of multi-token prediction (MTP) and speculative decoding to 3D structured languages is well-thought-out, particularly the relaxed distance metric (using tolerance threshold \tau) for continuous numerical coordinates.
The proposed Confidence-Guided Decoding (CGD) is a novel and elegant way to predict token reliability on the fly, eliminating the verification delay associated with traditional speculative decoding.

The parameter-efficient feature projection design successfully mitigates the heavy parameter overhead of naive MTP, making the model much more compact (~43% parameter reduction compared to standard MTP).
Extensive quantitative experiments on the ASE and Structured3D datasets, along with detailed ablation studies, demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of each proposed component.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental as multi-token prediction and speculative decoding are established techniques in the NLP domain. The primary contribution lies in their successful adaptation and refinement for structured spatial languages.

While SceneScript is designed as a multi-task generalist model (handling layout estimation, object detection, and part reconstruction), this work only evaluates on the 3D scene layout estimation task. Demonstrating the generalization of Fast SceneScript to other tasks would significantly strengthen the paper.
The performance and speedups depend on sensitive hyperparameters (such as \tau and the confidence threshold \epsilon), which may require task-specific tuning.

strengths: Significant and practical latency reduction: The proposed Fast SceneScript achieves a 5.09× to 5.57× speedup over the standard SceneScript model, addressing the critical bottleneck of autoregressive inference for structured 3D perception.

Domain-specific adaptation: Successfully adapts LLM acceleration techniques (multi-token prediction and speculative decoding) to structured language modeling by introducing a distance-based tolerance metric for numerical tokens (coordinates).
Parameter efficiency: The head-sharing and feature projection block design reduces the parameter overhead of multi-token prediction heads by ~43% while maintaining high accuracy.

Thorough evaluation: The paper contains solid quantitative experiments, comprehensive ablation studies, and informative analyses of the confidence distributions on both ASE and Structured3D benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited task evaluation: While SceneScript was proposed as a multi-task 3D perception generalist (handling layout estimation, 3D object detection, and part reconstruction), this work only evaluates the proposed acceleration on the 3D scene layout estimation task. Showing generalizability to other structured language outputs would significantly strengthen the paper.

Performance comparison of SSD vs. CGD: According to Tables 1 and 2, Self-Speculative Decoding (SSD) consistently outperforms the proposed Confidence-Guided Decoding (CGD) in terms of both inference latency and parameter efficiency, while maintaining comparable or better F1-scores. This makes the practical utility of the proposed CGD less convincing compared to the adapted SSD.

Incremental novelty: The core concepts of multi-token prediction, speculative decoding, and confidence-guided scoring are largely adopted from existing NLP/LLM literature (e.g., Medusa, Draft & Verify, etc.), with the primary adaptation being the distance metric for numerical tokens.

strengths: The paper targets a highly practical and significant bottleneck: the slow inference speed of autoregressive structured language models for 3D vision tasks.

The proposed adaptations for structured language—namely, using a distance-based tolerance threshold (τ) instead of strict exact matching for numerical tokens in speculative decoding—are highly intuitive and tailored to 3D coordinate outputs.
The proposed Confidence-Guided Decoding (CGD) provides an efficient, on-the-fly token verification method that avoids the verification overhead of standard speculative decoding.
The parameter-efficient projection and head-sharing mechanism successfully reduces parameter overhead by ~43% compared to standard MTP setups without sacrificing performance.
Strong empirical results on ASE and Structured3D datasets demonstrate a 5x speedup with comparable or even improved F1-scores.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted solely to the 3D scene layout estimation task. Since the original SceneScript model was proposed as a multi-task generalist (handling 3D object detection and part reconstruction), it is unclear how the proposed acceleration and decoding strategies generalize to these other tasks.

The core components (Multi-Token Prediction, Self-Speculative Decoding) are heavily borrowed from existing NLP/LLM literature (e.g., Medusa, DeepSeek). The novelty lies primarily in their domain-specific application and the numerical distance metric.

There is a lack of analysis regarding training overhead. The training process requires multiple stages (training NTP first, then MTP/CGD), but the paper does not discuss how much additional training time or computational resource this requires compared to standard NTP training.

The latency measurements are conducted on relatively old hardware (RTX 2080 Ti). It would be beneficial to see if the relative speedups hold when using more modern GPUs and software-level optimizations (such as TensorRT, FlashAttention, or torch.compile).

strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and critical bottleneck in language-based 3D scene understanding models: the slow inference speed caused by next-token autoregressive decoding.

The proposed adaptations for structured language models are highly sensible. Specifically, introducing a distance metric threshold for numerical tokens (e.g., coordinates) in self-speculative decoding (SSD) is an effective way to handle regression-like tasks in language formatting.

Confidence-guided decoding (CGD) is a novel and clever addition that predicts token reliability on the fly. This avoids the verification delay inherent in standard self-speculative decoding by modeling internal agreement between heads.

Strong empirical results are demonstrated across multiple synthetic and real-world indoor datasets (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD) for both 3D layout estimation and 3D object detection. The framework achieves ~5x speedup while maintaining or even slightly improving the F1-scores.
weaknesses: The core components of the method, such as Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) and speculative decoding, are well-established concepts in the natural language processing domain (e.g., Medusa, DeepSeek-V3). Thus, the architectural novelty is somewhat incremental, though the task-specific adaptations for 3D language-based models are valuable.

The latency measurements are reported on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti. It would be beneficial to provide benchmarks on more modern hardware (e.g., RTX 3090/4090 or A100/H100) to see if the speedup is sustained when memory bandwidth and compute boundaries shift.

The evaluation is primarily focused on upgrading the SceneScript framework. Demonstrating the generalizability of these speedup mechanisms on other structured-language 3D frameworks (e.g., SpatialLM) would further strengthen the paper's claims of being a general acceleration solution.

strengths: Significant inference acceleration (~5x speedup) for language-based 3D scene understanding models, which is crucial for real-time applicability.
Well-designed decoding strategies (SSD with numerical distance threshold, and CGD) tailored specifically for the structured language representations of 3D geometry.
Highly parameter-efficient design utilizing shared heads and lightweight projection blocks, which reduces the MTP decoder parameter overhead by ~43% compared to naive MTP.

Extensive evaluation on multiple synthetic and real-world benchmarks (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD) demonstrating consistent speedup and robust accuracy across layout estimation and object detection tasks.
Thorough ablation studies and intuitive analyses (such as softmax score distributions and token acceptance rates) that clearly explain the source of the improvements.
weaknesses: The performance and speedup of the proposed method rely on the quality of the base NTP prediction; if the model struggles with complex or out-of-distribution scenes, the token acceptance rate may drop, limiting the efficiency gains.

While layout estimation and object detection are thoroughly addressed, other tasks supported by SceneScript (such as 3D object part reconstruction) are not evaluated, leaving the generalizability of the proposed decoding strategies on tasks with different token structures unverified.

strengths: Addresses a critical bottleneck in language-based 3D scene understanding by significantly accelerating the autoregressive generation speed (achieving ~5x speedup).

Proposes a highly clever, domain-specific adaptation of speculative decoding for structured 3D language by incorporating a distance-based tolerance (τ) for numerical tokens (e.g., coordinates, height, width), which dramatically boosts token acceptance rates and latency reduction.

Introduces Confidence-Guided Decoding (CGD), an on-the-fly verification strategy that avoids verification delays in standard speculative decoding by learning to predict token consistency during training.
Features a parameter-efficient head-sharing design that reduces the MTP parameter overhead by over 40% compared to standard multi-head prediction, without sacrificing accuracy.

Provides extensive experiments and detailed ablations across multiple tasks (3D layout estimation, 3D object detection) and datasets (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD), confirming the robustness and generalizability of the proposed framework.
weaknesses: The formulation of the parameter-efficient shared projection block in Section 3.3 is slightly vague. From Figure 3, it appears to be a sequential/recurrent chain where the same projection block is applied to the previous hidden state (i.e., $f_{k+i} = \text{Proj}(f_{k+i-1})$), but this exact mathematical or conceptual flow is not explicitly written in the text.

Evaluation is largely conducted on synthetic datasets (ASE and Structured3D), and the real-world dataset (SceneCAD) has a relatively limited split size (1k training scenes). While this is a common limitation in the 3D structured language field, it restricts the ability to fully evaluate how the method scales to highly complex, large-scale real-world environments.
